summary: The note is a Wikipedia article on the tree line, the edge of a habitat beyond which trees cannot grow due to low temperatures, extreme snowpack, or lack of moisture. It covers causes (mean seasonal temperature near 6 °C, growing season requirements), types (alpine, exposure, arctic, Antarctic), tree species found near the tree line on each continent, and a table of approximate tree line elevations and latitudes worldwide. Navigation and reference boilerplate was ignored.
one_line: Wikipedia article describing the tree line, the high-elevation and high-latitude edge where trees can no longer grow, its causes, types, species and worldwide distribution.
key_facts: The tree line is the edge of a habitat at which trees are capable of growing and beyond which they are not, found at high elevations and high latitudes.
The tree line is approximately 300 to 1000 meters below the permanent snow line and roughly parallel to it.
The tree line follows the line where the seasonal mean temperature is approximately 6 °C or 43 °F.
A growing season of 94 days above 0.9 °C (33.6 °F) is required for tree growth.
At the tree line, tree growth is often sparse, stunted, and deformed by wind and cold, a form known as krummholz (German for 'crooked wood').
Treelines on north-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere are lower than on south-facing slopes because the increased shade means the snowpack takes longer to melt.
Snow accumulation in sheltered gullies in the Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia causes the tree line to be 400 metres (1,300 ft) lower than on exposed intervening shoulders.
Hawaii's treeline of about 8,000 ft (2,400 m) is above the condensation zone and results from a lack of moisture.
The arctic forest–tundra transition zone in northwestern Canada perhaps averages 145 kilometres (90 mi) in width.
Averaging over many locations, the treeline rises 75 metres (245 ft) per degree moving south from 70 to 50°N, and 130 metres (430 ft) per degree from 50 to 30°N.
Between 30°N and 20°S, the treeline is roughly constant, between 3,500 and 4,000 metres (11,500 and 13,100 ft).
The highest treeline in the world is on the slopes of Sajama Volcano in the Western Cordillera of the Bolivian Andes, formed by Polylepis tarapacana.
Antarctic Peninsula, at 63°S, has the mildest weather in Antarctica yet no trees survive there, only mosses, lichens, and grasses.
The Aleutian Islands are almost completely treeless due to the Oyashio Current and strong winds affecting summer temperatures.
Campbell Island (52°S) is treeless except for one stunted Spruce planted by scientists.
